back: If the network can partition, a replicated system cannot guarantee both linearizability and that every non-failing node responds, during that partition.
Linearizability: behaves like one copy; once a read returns a value, every later read returns it or newer. Not ACID's C.
Every request to a non-failing node eventually gets a non-error response, with no time bound, on every side of a partition. Stricter than SLA uptime.
Conjectured by Eric Brewer (2000 keynote); proved by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch (2002).
Partitions happen to you. The real choice is what each operation does when one occurs: refuse (C) or answer possibly stale (A).

front: Why does a GC pause count as a partition?
back: Peers can't tell a paused node from a cut-off one: both just miss replies past the timeout.
A timeout decision: after waiting, proceed alone (favour A) or refuse (favour C).
Only the 3-node majority side. The 2-node side can't commit writes or serve linearizable reads.

front: How can a 'CP' leader serve a stale read?
back: It is cut off and deposed but still answers reads from memory. Fix: confirm leadership with a majority (read index) before reading.
Per query. CL ONE keeps every side answering (AP-like); QUORUM reads and writes refuse on the minority side (CP-like).
Stays writable on every side and merges conflicting versions, so a deleted item can occasionally reappear.
P isn't optional; the choice is per operation, not all-or-nothing; it ignores latency on a healthy network.
If Partition: Availability or Consistency. Else: Latency or Consistency.
PA/EL by default (Abadi's classification): available under partition, low latency otherwise.

front: Cost of a consistent write with leader in Virginia and quorum in Europe?
back: At least one cross-Atlantic round trip, roughly 75–90 ms, on every write.
